Q: What Is the Actual Maximum Argument Length for Process.Start? A:

According to Raymon Chen, one of the senior developers of Windows:

It depends on whom you ask.

The maximum command line length for the CreateProcess function is 32767 characters. This limitation comes from the UNICODE_STRING structure. CreateProcess is the core function for creating processes, so if you are talking directly to Win32, then that’s the only limit you have to worry about.

But if you are reaching CreateProcess by some other means, then the path you travel through may have other limits. ... If you are using the ShellExecute/Ex function, then you become subject to the INTERNET_MAX_URL_LENGTH (around 2048) command line length limit imposed by the ShellExecute/Ex functions.

UseShellExecute = true uses, as you might imagine, the ShellExecuteExW function. But in this case, anything over 2048 is truncated silently.

UseShellExecute = false uses CreateProcessWithLogonW, which is similar to CreateProcessW.

Q: Counting continuous membership in SQL A:

I suggest looking at a solution using bitmasks.
Since you are talking about 16 months, most likely the data structure is different and the year is present. However, in a simplified way, we can consider an example with 4 months. There is no fundamental difference. "bitmask" approach is usually criticized for the inability to use indexes. But in this case, there is no such drawback.
Using a bitmask will significantly reduce the amount of data processed. In your example you SELF JOIN table with 32M rows with triangular condition. 2Mx0.8 for each pair of month (1616/2=128 pairs)

In the first step, we consolidate the data to 1 row per MemberID. It is possible to estimate the reduction of data from 16x2M=32M rows -> 2M+(2Mx0.2)x15=8M rows (distinct members).

member_month0 as(   
SELECT MemberID, 
   sum(case when Month='January' then 1   -- January,
            when Month='February' then 2  -- February,
            when Month='March' then 4     -- March
            when Month='April' then 8     -- March
       else 0 
       end) AS  MemberMonthsMask
FROM test
GROUP BY MemberID
)

The next step is to combine (count the number of) MemberId's with the same bitmasks. This will reduce data size. (estimate) If we assume that 20% of memberids are lost every month and 20% new ones appear, we can estimate the number of rows 2M+(2M/16)x15 ~ 3.9M

monMask_counts as(
SELECT MemberMonthsMask,count(*) member_count
FROM member_month t
GROUP BY MemberMonthsMask
)

Next, let's move on to the output result. I use CTE to list all the months.

 all_months as (
   SELECT * from (
     VALUES ('January',1,1),('February',2,2),('March',3,4),('April',4,8) 
     )t(month,nm,mask)
)

The SELF JOIN of this auxiliary table (CTE) is in the form of a triangular join (ON mm2.nm>mm1.nm).

SELECT concat(mm1.month,cast(mm1.nm as varchar)) monthA,concat(mm2.month,cast(mm2.nm as varchar)) monthB
  ,mmc.member_count
FROM all_months mm1 
INNER JOIN all_months mm2 ON mm2.nm>mm1.nm
LEFT JOIN monMask_counts mmc ON (mmc.MemberMonthsMask & mm1.mask)<>0 
                            and (mmc.MemberMonthsMask & mm2.mask)<>0

For example data

INSERT INTO test (Month, MemberID) VALUES
    ('January', '100'),
    ('January', '101'),
    ('January', '103'),
    ('January', '104'),
    ('January', '105'),
    ('February', '100'),
    ('February', '102'),
    ('February', '103'),
    ('February', '104'),
    ('March', '100'),
    ('March', '105');

we will get the result

 monthA   |  monthB   | member_count 
-----------+-----------+--------------
 January1  | February2 |            2
 January1  | February2 |            1
 January1  | March3    |            1
 January1  | March3    |            1
 January1  | April4    |             
 February2 | March3    |            1
 February2 | April4    |

Q: implement case when statement with dict items and two column values, return true if match A:

Convert dic into a list of strings by joining its elements using a specified separator string (####); similarly, join the values ​​in the nameand id columns using the same separator; finally, use the isin function to compare whether the two resulting lists are identical.

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

...
str_ls = [i[0] + '####' + str(i[1]) for i in dic]
df = df.select('*', F.when(F.concat('name', F.lit('####'), 'id').isin(str_ls), True).otherwise(False).alias('flag'))
df.show()

Q: Can a individual man in their 30's without completing any academic degree's still do well in the data analyst field? A:

I have known many successful software engineers who did not have a degree in a computer-related field. They may have a degree in some other field, or even no degree.

But it's harder to get through the interview process. Many companies filter out people who don't have a relevant degree, because they get hundreds of candidates and they have to filter them out somehow. In the US, jobs in the government or in companies who contract with the government are even more strict about this. So you may have limited choice of your potential employers.

Regarding learning new job skills, it's a challenge for people in their thirties or older to devote time to studying and practicing skills for any new career (computer or otherwise), because we tend to get more responsibilities like home and family as we get older. Time becomes scarce.

Even if you get into the career, you might find it awkward to work with younger coworkers. Consider you will be in your thirties, working with people ten years younger than you who still have more relevant experience. You have to continually remind yourself not to compare yourself to others, and just be happy to learn from teammates and don't be embarrassed that you're not their senior. That's not a failure on your part if they started younger.

So it is possible, but in some ways it's more challenging to change careers the older we get. It's up to you to commit yourself and stick with it.
